handsOnLab.brief: You will build a complete Detect alert runbook for three alert types and then triage five sample alerts against it, producing verdicts with documented reasoning. This is the SOC-analyst muscle: consistent triage from a written standard.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every sample alert has a verdict, reasoning, and evidence cited; the runbook covers all three alert types with escalation criteria.
handsOnLab.deliverable: detect-runbook.md plus triage-decisions.md — the standard and five worked triages.
steps: Define your three alert types: (1) blocked application execution (allowlist deny), (2) blocked child-process spawn (ringfence deny), (3) blocked storage/network attempt (storage or network deny).

For each type, write the runbook section: trigger description, default severity, context to gather (process, parent, user, machine, time, history), triage steps in order, verdict branches (benign / policy violation / incident), and escalation criteria.
Set the SLAs: triage start time per severity (e.g., critical 15 min, high 1 hr, medium 4 hr) and document them in the runbook.
Write the MDR handoff template: fields for who/what/when/where, blocked action with context, checks completed, evidence links, and the specific ask.
Now triage sample alert 1: 'Blocked execution of invoice_helper.exe (unsigned, temp folder) on ACCOUNTING-07, user m.reyes, 9:02 AM.' Write the verdict with reasoning.
Triage sample alert 2: 'Blocked child-process spawn: winword.exe attempted powershell.exe on ACCOUNTING-07, user m.reyes, 9:02 AM, encoded arguments.' Write the verdict with reasoning.
Triage sample alert 3: 'Blocked USB mass-storage write on WORKSTATION-23, user j.chen, files: client_master.xlsx, 6:47 PM, third occurrence this week.' Write the verdict with reasoning.
Triage sample alert 4: 'Blocked outbound HTTPS from unknown process update_svc.exe on IT-04, 2:14 AM, destination unlisted.' Write the verdict with reasoning.
Triage sample alert 5: 'Blocked registry write (Run key) by allowed PDF reader on SALES-11, user t.okafor, 11:30 AM.' Write the verdict with reasoning.
Review all five triages: confirm each cites evidence (not gut feeling), each follows the runbook's steps, and each ends with a concrete next action.
Write the tuning note: which of the five alert types would you baseline or suppress after 30 days of data, and what documented rule would you write.
handsOnLab.title: Detect alert runbook + five triages

notes.body: ThreatLocker Detect is the module that turns prevention into intelligence: it alerts on the indicators of compromise that the other modules blocked. Every denied execution, every fenced child-process spawn, every blocked USB write and every denied lateral connection emits an alert carrying the full context — the process, its parent chain, the user, the machine, the timestamp, and exactly which policy said no. Understand why this inverts the traditional SOC experience. In a detection-first world (classic EDR), the sensor watches the attack run and tries to recognize malice in progress: behavioral analytics, machine-learning scores, threat-intel matches. The alert says, in effect, 'something looks 73% malicious, please investigate while it continues.' Analysts drown in probabilistic leads, most benign, and the true positives arrive while the damage is underway. In the prevention-first world, the enforcement already stopped the attempt — the alert says 'this specific action was attempted and denied,' which is a statement of fact, not a probability. A blocked child-process spawn from Word at 9:02 AM is not 73% suspicious; it is an attempted attack step, caught red-handed, with the evidence attached. This is why prevention-first alerts are higher fidelity: the enforcement decision pre-filters the noise. The benign application that behaves normally never triggers; the malicious step triggers by attempting the forbidden. Worked example: compare the two SOC mornings. Detection-first SOC: 400 alerts overnight — 380 benign (updaters, admin tools, user oddities scored as suspicious), 15 duplicates, 5 worth reading, 1 real. The analyst's morning is triage-as-archaeology, and the real one is buried. Prevention-first SOC: 12 alerts overnight — each a blocked action with full context. The analyst reads 12 factual events, clears 8 as benign-with-reason (stale hash rule, approved updater), and escalates 4 with evidence. Same company, same threats, radically different signal-to-noise — because the blocks did the filtering. Common gotcha: 'fewer alerts means less visibility.' The opposite: the prevented attempts are the highest-value visibility you can get — malice confirmed at the attempt stage, before damage. The SOC's job shifts from finding needles in haystacks to judging 12 needles, which is a job humans can actually do well. Second gotcha: treating Detect as 'just logging.' The alert pipeline — severity, routing, SLA, runbook — is what makes the blocks operationally useful. Blocks without triage are security theater with receipts.  Design the alert routing before the alerts arrive. Critical-severity alerts page the on-call analyst; high-severity alerts land in the priority queue with a one-hour triage SLA; everything else flows to the standard queue. Route by asset criticality too — the domain controller's medium is the kiosk's critical. And build the queue dashboards around the runbook's verdicts, not raw counts: 'alerts triaged to incident this week' is a security metric, 'total alerts' is just weather. The routing design is what keeps the 2 AM alert from waiting until 9 AM.
notes.title: What Detect is: the block becomes the signal

notes.body: Every alert gets the same five-input triage, in the same order, because consistency is what makes a SOC defensible and auditable. Input one: severity. The alert's initial severity comes from the policy that fired and the action blocked — a blocked unsigned execution in temp is higher severity than a blocked updater with a stale rule. Severity sets the SLA clock: critical starts triage in minutes, medium in hours. Input two: asset criticality. The same block on the domain controller and on a kiosk are different events — know your crown jewels (finance workstations, servers, executive machines, IT admin boxes) and weight accordingly. Input three: user and role context. Who was at the keyboard? The finance user's blocked macro at 9 AM during month-end reads differently than the same block on a service account at 3 AM. Check whether the user is where they should be, doing what they should do. Input four: the blocked action's details. Read the actual event: which process, which parent, what was attempted, what was the target, what arguments were passed? Encoded PowerShell arguments are a different universe from a missing file path. Input five: pattern history. Has this user, this machine, this process generated similar alerts? One blocked USB write is curiosity; three in a week across machines is intent. The verdict has three branches. Benign: the block was correct but harmless — stale rule, approved tool, user error. Action: fix the rule or educate the user, document, close. Policy violation without malice: the user tried to bypass policy for convenience. Action: document, retrain, check whether a broken legitimate workflow drove it. Incident: real attack attempt or suspicious pattern. Action: escalate per the runbook — isolate, preserve, investigate. Worked example: the 9:02 AM alert from M01. Severity: high (blocked child-process spawn, encoded args). Asset: accounting workstation (crown jewel — finance data). User: m.reyes, finance, at her desk at 9 AM (context fits). Action details: winword.exe → powershell.exe, encoded command line (malicious pattern). History: first alert for this user/machine. Verdict: incident — isolate ACCOUNTING-07, preserve the logs, escalate to IR. The triage took the five inputs in order and produced a defensible verdict in minutes. Common gotcha: verdict before context. Reading the alert title and deciding 'it's just the updater' without checking the arguments is how real intrusions get closed as benign. The workflow's order exists to prevent exactly this. Second gotcha: severity as destiny. Initial severity starts the clock; the triage determines the verdict. A 'medium' alert with a malicious pattern history becomes an incident — let the inputs move the verdict.
notes.title: The alert triage workflow: five inputs, three verdicts

notes.body: Prevention-first versus detection-first is the architectural debate underneath every EDR conversation, and you should be able to argue it from the operator's chair. Detection-first (traditional EDR) assumes the attack will run: the sensor monitors process behavior, network flows, and file activity, and tries to recognize malice while it executes. Its strengths are real: it catches fileless attacks, it sees the techniques that prevention misses, and its telemetry is invaluable for hunting. Its structural weakness is time: recognition happens during or after the malicious action, so the SOC races the attacker — and the attacker only needs to be faster than the analyst's queue. Prevention-first (Detect's model) assumes the attempt can be stopped: the policy denies the malicious action before it executes, and the denial becomes the alert. Its strength is the timeline: the SOC starts at the attempt stage, with the attack already dead. Its honest limitation is coverage: prevention stops what policy forbids, so novel techniques outside the fenced behaviors still need detection — which is why the mature design is prevention-first with detection depth, not prevention-only. The dwell-time argument needs care: you will hear claims about average attacker dwell times, but do not quote numbers you cannot source. The structural argument needs no numbers: an alert at the attempt stage is earlier than an alert at the damage stage, by construction. Worked example: the same intrusion against both architectures. Detection-first: the attacker lands, the EDR scores the behavior, an alert fires mid-encryption, the analyst starts triage while files encrypt — the race is on. Prevention-first: the attacker's first malicious step (the child-process spawn) is denied at 9:02:14, the alert fires at 9:02:15 with the attack dead — the analyst triages a corpse, calmly, with full evidence. The incident still gets investigated (how did the document arrive? are there others?), but nobody is racing encryption. Common gotcha: presenting prevention-first as making detection obsolete. It does not — it changes detection's job from 'catch the attack in progress' to 'judge the attempts and hunt what policy missed.' The SOC still hunts; it just hunts from a position of already having stopped the bleeding. Second gotcha: assuming prevented means uninteresting. The blocked attempt is the highest-quality threat intelligence the company produces — it names the attacker's current tools, targets, and timing. Feed it to the threat-intel process, not just the ticket queue.  Close the loop between triage and prevention. Every incident verdict should produce at least one candidate policy improvement: a new ringfence behavior to deny, an allowlist rule to tighten, an egress destination to remove. Track these as follow-up tickets owned by the policy team, not as informal suggestions — the SOC sees the attacks, the policy team owns the gates, and the feedback ticket is the bridge. A SOC whose findings never change policy is an expensive observation deck.
notes.title: Detect vs traditional EDR: prevention-first vs detection-first

notes.body: When an alert exceeds your authority, evidence, or expertise, it goes to the managed detection and response provider — and the quality of your handoff determines the quality of their response. The MDR handoff is a package, not a forward: it contains everything the MDR analyst needs to act without re-doing your triage. The package has six fields. Who/what/when/where: user, machine, timestamp, alert ID — the identifiers that let them pull their own telemetry. The blocked action with full context: which policy fired, which process and parent, what was attempted, the arguments or targets — the factual core. What you already checked: the triage steps completed and their results — 'verified the binary hash against the vendor's published value: no match' saves them an hour. Your verdict and reasoning: incident-suspected, with the two or three facts that drove it — they will form their own judgment, but they deserve your read. The evidence links: alert IDs, log locations, ticket numbers — no 'the logs are somewhere in the console.' The specific ask: what you need — 'please confirm whether this hash appears in your wider telemetry' or 'requesting containment approval for these three machines.' Worked example: the 2 AM unknown-process alert. Handoff: 'ACCOUNTING-07, user m.reyes, 02:14 — blocked outbound HTTPS from update_svc.exe (unsigned, temp path) to unlisted destination. Checked: binary not in allowlist, hash unknown to reputation, parent is a scheduled task created yesterday, user states they were asleep. Verdict: suspected intrusion — the process identity, timing, and persistence mechanism all indicate malice. Evidence: alert DET-8841, process tree in ticket IR-2203. Ask: please check your telemetry for this hash across our estate and advise on containment scope.' That handoff gets action in minutes; a bare alert forward gets questions for an hour. The escalation criteria in your runbook define when the handoff happens: suspected incidents go immediately, pattern-level suspicions go with the pattern summary, and anything involving crown-jewel assets goes faster. Common gotcha: handoff as abdication. The MDR extends your team; it does not replace your triage. A handoff that says 'please investigate this alert' with no context is a confession that you skipped the workflow. Second gotcha: no feedback loop. When the MDR closes the case, their verdict comes back into your runbook — the tuning, the new detection, the lessons learned. Handoffs without feedback are a treadmill.  Set handoff SLAs with the MDR provider in the contract, not in the crisis. Define the severity-to-response-time mapping, the escalation path when the SLA is missed, and the format of the verdict that comes back — because the feedback is what tunes your runbook. Review the handoff quality quarterly with real tickets: were the packages complete, were the asks specific, did the verdicts come back in time to act? The MDR relationship is operated like any vendor relationship: measured, reviewed, and improved.
notes.title: MDR handoff: packaging the alert for action

notes.body: The runbook is the module's deliverable because it makes triage a property of the organization, not of whoever happens to be on shift. A Detect alert runbook has six parts, and you will write one in the lab. Part one: the trigger — which alert, from which policy, in plain language ('blocked child-process spawn from an Office application'). Part two: default severity and SLA — how fast triage starts. Part three: context to gather — the exact fields and where to find them (process, parent chain, user, machine, time, the user's alert history). Part four: triage steps in order — the five-input workflow from this module, written as checkable steps. Part five: verdict branches — what benign, violation, and incident each look like for this alert type, with two or three concrete examples per branch. Part six: escalation criteria — exactly when this goes to the MDR, to IR, or to management, with the handoff package template attached. Worked example: the runbook section for 'blocked USB mass-storage write.' Trigger: storage policy deny on removable-media write. Severity: medium default; high if finance/engineering asset or repeat pattern. Context: device ID and registration status, user and role, file paths and byte counts, the user's 30-day alert history. Triage: check registration (registered drive blocked = possible stale exception), check the files (sensitive paths raise severity), check history (pattern = intent). Verdicts: benign — new hire unaware of policy, first occurrence, non-sensitive files (action: educate, close). Violation — repeat attempts, no malice indicators (action: retrain, check workflow gap). Incident — sensitive targets, multiple machines, off-hours, or combined with other module alerts (action: isolate, preserve, escalate to IR). Escalation: any incident-verdict goes to IR immediately; any pattern of three-plus attempts goes to the security lead same-day. The runbook also carries the tuning section: after 30 days, which alerts proved benign-by-pattern get documented suppressions — each suppression naming the pattern, the owner, and the review date. Common gotcha: the runbook as shelfware. A runbook nobody opens during triage is documentation theater — it must be short enough to use mid-incident, linked from the alert itself, and updated every time a triage teaches something new. Second gotcha: verdict branches without examples. 'Use your judgment' is not a branch — the examples are what let a junior analyst triage like a senior at 3 AM.  Version the runbook and review it on a schedule — monthly for the active sections, quarterly cover to cover. Every triage that teaches something new produces a runbook update: a new example in a verdict branch, a tightened escalation criterion, a new tuning rule. Keep a changelog so analysts can see what changed and why; a runbook that silently mutates loses trust. The review meeting is short when the changelog does the talking: what did we learn, what did we change, what needs re-tuning.
notes.title: Building the Detect alert runbook

notes.body: Alert fatigue is the SOC's chronic illness: too many alerts, too little signal, analysts skimming, real incidents missed in the noise. Prevention-first architectures start with an advantage — the blocks pre-filter — but the advantage erodes without tuning discipline. The tuning program has four parts. Baselining: for the first 30-60 days, every alert type gets its benign rate measured — which alerts fire, how often, and what fraction prove benign. You cannot tune what you have not measured. Documented suppression: benign-by-pattern alerts get suppression rules — but every suppression is a written decision naming the pattern, the evidence it is benign, the owner, and the review date. 'We suppressed updater blocks' is blindness; 'we suppress blocks where the binary is vendor-signed, the hash matches the vendor's published value, and the parent is the approved updater — owner: SOC lead, review: quarterly' is tuning. Anomaly preservation: suppressions target known-benign patterns only — anything novel, anything from a new process, anything off-pattern still fires. The day the 'known-benign' updater behaves differently is the day you want the alert. Review cadence: suppressions expire and are re-justified on schedule, because vendors get compromised and benign patterns change. Worked example: the updater-block tuning. Week one: 40 alerts — 'blocked execution of vendor updater, hash mismatch.' Triage shows the vendor rotated their signing certificate; the binaries are legitimate. Suppression written: allow the new certificate for the updater product, scoped, owner named, 90-day review. Alerts drop to zero for this pattern — legitimately, because the policy now reflects reality. Contrast with the lazy version: 'suppress all updater alerts' — which would also suppress the trojaned updater next quarter. The case walkthrough that ties the module together: the full M01 attack as a Detect story. 9:02:14 — blocked child-process spawn (winword.exe → powershell.exe), severity high, full context attached. 9:02:15 — blocked file write to temp. 9:02:16 — blocked unknown execution. Three alerts, one incident, one timeline: the SOC sees the attacker's playbook in the order it was attempted, each step already dead. The analyst's job is verdict and scope (how did the document arrive? any other recipients?), not a race against encryption. That is the prevention-first SOC: fewer alerts, each factual, triaged at the attempt stage. Common gotcha: tuning by volume instead of by pattern. 'Reduce alerts by 50%' as a goal produces blind suppressions; 'every alert type has a measured benign rate and a documented disposition' produces a tuned SOC. Second gotcha: the hero analyst who 'just knows.' Institutionalize the knowledge in the runbook — heroes go on vacation, runbooks do not.
notes.title: Alert fatigue, tuning, and the full attack as a Detect story
